author: NorthEast News Desk
body: Rhode Island artists and artist groups can now apply for a new grant program intended to turn climate information into public-facing art, stories and experiences. The Rhode Island State Council on the Arts, working with the Executive Climate Change Coordinating Council Advisory Board, opened applications Oct. 1 for the Arts and Climate Grant. The application deadline is Nov. 2 at 11:59 p.m., according to RISCA’s [grant guidelines](https://arts.ri.gov/grants/arts-and-climate).

The program is designed for projects that help residents understand climate change and participate in conversations about how communities should respond. RISCA says eligible work can address mitigation topics such as energy-efficient buildings, renewable energy, public transit, electric vehicles and heat pumps, or resilience issues such as flooding, extreme heat, stronger storms, sea-level rise, wetlands and community resilience hubs. The goal is not simply to decorate a climate campaign; the agency says artists may act as community connectors who gather local perspectives and carry those experiences back to state climate planners.

Awards can be as large as $5,000, although the grant page warns that partial awards are common. A partial award must be at least half of the request or $1,000, whichever is higher. The money is intended for projects taking place in Rhode Island between Jan. 1 and Dec. 30, 2027. RISCA expects to notify applicants in mid-December, with final reports due Jan. 31, 2028. The first cycle is backed by $40,000 that the EC4 Advisory Board allocated to its partnership with RISCA from an $80,000 climate-communication award, according to the [program description](https://arts.ri.gov/grants/arts-and-climate).

The eligibility rules place the emphasis on Rhode Island residents working as the primary artistic force behind their projects. Applicants must be at least 18, have lived in the state for at least one year and be legally resident in the United States with a tax identification number. Groups of artists may apply, but the work must be artist-instigated and organized outside an institution’s formal program. Projects may include a public performance, exhibition, curriculum, video, mural, brochure or other format, but RISCA says a pilot or public sharing is required when the proposal involves planning or curriculum development.

The program’s structure reflects a practical problem in climate policy: technical plans can be difficult to understand even when they describe changes that affect daily life. Rhode Island’s climate agencies are working across issues that residents encounter locally, from coastal flooding and stormwater to home energy costs, transportation and heat. RISCA says projects should prioritize frontline communities, include community voices and use two-way engagement. That gives artists room to work at a neighborhood scale rather than requiring a statewide campaign or a large institutional production.

The funding also comes with limits. Grants cannot pay for capital construction or renovations, debt, regranting, prizes or events that are inaccessible to the public. Applicants cannot use the program for work that is part of an undergraduate or graduate degree, and they cannot seek support for the same project through another RISCA grant, except for the agency’s general operating support for artists. Awardees must credit RISCA and the EC4 Advisory Board in their marketing materials.

RISCA will offer an online information session Oct. 6 from 3 to 4 p.m. and another Oct. 14 from 6 to 7 p.m., followed by drop-in support hours later in October and on the deadline day. The Oct. 6 session will include an overview, a walkthrough of the application and time for questions, according to the [event listing](https://arts.ri.gov/events/arts-and-climate-grant-information-session). Applications are submitted through RISCA’s online grant system. Questions about the program can be sent to risca.contact@arts.ri.gov.

The grant is administered by RISCA, but its climate-policy connection runs through EC4, the state council established under Rhode Island’s climate laws to coordinate mitigation and adaptation work. The [EC4 Advisory Board](https://climatechange.ri.gov/ri-executive-climate-change-coordinating-council-ec4/advisory-board) includes municipal representatives and members with expertise in economic policy, workforce development, natural and cultural resources, energy, education, public health and housing. The new grant therefore creates a small but concrete channel for residents’ creative work to inform the state’s broader resilience conversation.
dek: The new program will fund artist-led projects that make climate information more accessible, with applications due Nov. 2 and work scheduled for 2027.
